title: The rhythm of the tides
paragraphs: On the west coast, the tide transforms the everyday map of usable ground. Flats that appear as shallow water become extensive stretches of mud and sand when the sea retreats. These environments offer shellfish, small fish, salt-making possibilities, and routes that change with the hour. Later communities used knowledge of tidal cycles as a practical form of expertise. A person unfamiliar with the channels could mistake an apparently easy crossing for a dangerous passage.

A tidal flat is also a workplace, not merely a scenic landscape. Gathering food, locating safe routes, moving boats, and observing seasonal changes demand close attention to local conditions. Such settings connect environmental history to the history of labor and household life. Even when written records are scarce, the coast itself helps explain why water-based livelihoods developed unevenly around the peninsula.
